 Millions of Retirees Are Getting a Big 2027 COLA - But Experts Say the Formula Shortchanges Seniors
 Social Security benefits are getting a big increase in 2027, but your raise may not go as far as expected.
 By
 Maurie Backman 
 ,
 Edited by
 Laura Hohenstein 
 Updated
 Nov. 2, 2026
 Fact checked 
 This article was subjected to a comprehensive fact-checking process. Our professional fact-checkers verify article information against primary sources, reputable publishers, and experts in the field.
 Add Us On Google
 Google Preferred Sources lets you customize your search results. By choosing to follow FinanceBuzz, you’re telling Google to prioritize content from a source you trust.
Social Security is one of the most important senior benefits 
today. There are some who end up collecting Social Security for 
decades in retirement without any other income to fall back on. That's what 
makes the program's cost-of-living adjustments, or COLAs, so important. 
Each year, Social Security benefits are eligible for a COLA that's tied to 
inflation. Previously, Congress had to vote on COLAs individually, but 
now, those raises come in automatically when inflation warrants an increase. 
The Social Security Administration recently announced that the 2027 COLA is 3.6%, but here's why seniors may not want to celebrate that raise just yet.

 What a 3.6% COLA could do for the average Social Security check
Last year, Social Security benefits received a 2.8% COLA. This year's 3.6% 
increase is a lot larger and could add a nice amount of money to seniors' 
benefit checks.
 For instance, the average monthly Social Security retirement benefit today is about $2,089. So 
a 3.6% COLA results in a monthly boost of around $75. On a yearly basis, that's 
an extra $900 for the typical retiree.
Of course, this does not account for any increases in the cost of Medicare Part 
B. Seniors who are enrolled in both Medicare and Social Security pay their Part 
B premiums out of their monthly benefits automatically. If the cost of Part B 
goes up a lot in 2027, it could eat into the upcoming COLA.

 How Social Security COLAs are calculated
You may be wondering how Social Security calculates your annual COLA. Those 
raises are based on changes to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical 
Workers (CPI-W) during the third quarter of the year.
When there's an increase in the CPI-W during that time, Social Security benefits 
go up. If the CPI-W shows a decrease in annual inflation during the third 
quarter of the year, benefits stay where they are. They can't decrease from year 
to year. 
 Why the current COLA formula fails seniors
The problem with the current COLA formula is that it's based on an index that 
does not accurately reflect the real-world costs Social Security recipients 
face. The CPI-W may do a good job of capturing price changes for 
 workers , but retirees on Social Security tend to spend their money very 
differently. 
Because of this problematic formula, the Senior Citizens League says Social 
Security recipients have lost out on a lot of buying power over time. Since 
2016, benefits have shed 13.7% of their purchasing power, and that trend could 
continue if a change to the COLA formula isn't made. This mismatch could easily 
render the 2027 Social Security COLA less effective even though it's a pretty 
large increase in its own right.

 What lawmakers can do to make COLAs more effective
Shifting the Social Security COLA formula to better match seniors' real-world 
expenses and cost increases could help benefits better maintain their buying 
power in the future. Advocates have long pushed for COLAs to be based on the 
Consumer Price Index for the Elderly so that senior-specific costs are accounted 
for. 
However, Congress is currently tasked with preventing Social Security cuts, 
which could happen as early as 2032, according to a recent update from the 
program's Trustees. Lawmakers may not have the capacity to deal with changes to 
the COLA formula as they try to shore up Social Security's finances broadly. 
Plus, a change that results in larger COLAs for seniors only puts more pressure 
on Social Security's limited financial resources. So that's another reason 
Social Security recipients shouldn't expect an updated COLA formula anytime 
soon. If the formula were to get an adjustment in the near term, it could push 
Social Security closer to broad cuts, ultimately leaving seniors with less money 
overall. 
 Bottom line
Your Social Security benefits may be a big part of your retirement plan . It may be ideal to be getting a 3.6% COLA in the new year, but it's important to 
note that the increase might not hold up well to inflation, especially if 
prices start to rise substantially in the new year. 
Also, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates by a quarter of a percentage 
point in September, which means that if you have variable-interest debt, like 
credit card balances, your monthly payments could climb. And any new borrowing 
you do in 2027 could also be more expensive. 
Given all of this, you may want to rethink your financial plans for 2027 and not 
bank on your upcoming COLA too heavily. If you're worried money may be tight, 
it's worth seeing if you could work part-time to supplement your Social Security 
checks. You're allowed to work while collecting Social Security, and the 
thresholds for earning money before having benefits withheld are increasing in 
2027, giving you even more leeway to earn some extra money.
